tldr: The authors propose PAMoR, a diffusion-based motion generation framework for humanoid robots that uses affect parameters (valence and arousal) computed directly from kinematics to modulate emotional expression in real time while preserving the original action semantics.
hero_caption: Overview of PAMoR. Top-left shows data processing and kinematics-based automatic V-A labeling. The bottom shows how text (action content) and V/A (affective expression) are combined compositionally as separate diffusion priors. Top-right shows real-time motion rollout on the physical Unitree G1 robot.
overview:
Humanoid robots living alongside humans need to convey appropriate emotion and nuance through their gestures, not just execute assigned physical tasks. However, existing affective motion generation has focused on virtual human avatars. These methods rely on style transfer from reference clips or emotion words inside text prompts, making quantitative and explainable parametric control difficult. Furthermore, retargeting avatar-oriented motions onto physical robots causes latency and distorts posture extension and velocity, which are essential for affective expression.

To tackle this, the authors built PAMoR, a framework that uses the valence-arousal (V-A) emotional coordinate plane—computed directly from robot forward kinematics—as a measured control parameter. Valence is calculated analytically from postural expansion, and arousal from movement energy, creating labeled training data automatically without human annotation. In addition, PAMoR adopts composable latent diffusion: an action prior that decides what to do and two affect priors (V and A) that modulate how to perform it are trained independently in a shared latent space and composed during sampling.

In experiments on a 29-DoF Unitree G1, PAMoR generated a 400 ms motion primitive in 78 ms, demonstrating real-time performance with on-the-fly editing of both action prompts and affect parameters. In a perceptual user study, raters correctly identified the commanded emotion from the faceless robot's body motion alone on 38% of trials, approaching the 44% recognition rate reported for acted human bodies and demonstrating high expressive fidelity.
contributions: A closed-form labeling method grounded in body language literature that computes continuous V-A affect coordinates directly from robot forward kinematics without human annotation

A composable latent diffusion model that trains the action text prior and continuous scalar affect priors separately in a shared latent space and fuses them at sampling time, enabling real-time editing without action collapse
Demonstration of real-time rollout and accurate tracking across the entire continuous affect plane while preserving action semantics on a physical 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid
Validation via a perceptual user study showing an affect recognition rate that approaches human performance on acted body movements

sections.heading: Bridging Robot Motion Generation and Affective Expression
sections.summary: While text-driven motion generation has advanced toward native physical humanoid synthesis, continuous affect control has remained unexplored. This work addresses the challenge by grounding composable diffusion models and dimensional emotion theory directly in robot kinematics.
sections.details:
Motion diffusion models for robotics have recently shifted from generating for human avatars to native synthesis directly in robot-specific spaces (such as ECHO and TextOp). Retargeting avatar motions onto robots not only introduces latency into the inference loop, but also distorts postural tension and movement speed, which are central to conveying emotion. However, existing native robot generation methods remain restricted to text-specified action content and do not address parametric affect control.

Meanwhile, emotional motion generation has traditionally relied on style transfer from reference videos or emotion labels within text. These approaches tightly entangle action content with emotional style, making it difficult to control expression at an intended intensity. While some prior robotics studies explored the V-A plane on low-DoF platforms, real-time continuous rollout on full-body bipedal humanoids was still missing.

This work turns to Russell's circumplex model (the V-A plane) from psychology. Empirical human observation studies have established that postural expansion (e.g., puffing out the chest, opening the arms) conveys positive valence, while movement energy such as velocity and acceleration conveys arousal. While prior work used this mapping mainly to train emotion classifiers, PAMoR breaks new ground by formulating it into explicit kinematic equations on the robot and using those measurements directly as control signals for generative modeling.

sections.heading: Quantifying Affect from Body Kinematics and Composing Three Priors
sections.summary: The authors present an automatic labeling method that calculates V-A coordinates in closed form from joint geometry, along with a composable diffusion model that blends action (text) and affect (V and A) as independent priors.
sections.details:
The motion representation $\mathbf{x}_t$ in this framework is a vector stacking root pose, linear translation, foot contact flags, root height, joint angles, and joint angular velocities. Given a history $\mathbf{h}$ of the past $H$ frames, a text prompt $\tau$, and target affect coordinates $(v,a) \in [-1,1]^2$, the model autoregressively predicts the future $F$ frames.

First, for automatic V-A labeling (III-B), the method extracts 14 primary keypoints via forward kinematics. Valence is defined as postural expansion, computed by normalizing and summing three metrics: the perimeter of the triangle formed by the wrists and torso (lateral expansion), root height (vertical extension), and torso pitch angle (forward hunching versus chest-up posture). Arousal is defined as movement energy, calculated as the sum of mean velocity and mean acceleration across all keypoints. These values are Winsorized to handle outliers and scaled to $[-1, 1]$, producing interpretable affect labels without human annotation.

For generation, the framework uses a composable latent diffusion model (III-C). A 9-layer Transformer Motion VAE (MVAE) first compresses motion data into 128-dimensional latent tokens $\mathbf{z}$. Conditioning a single model on text, V, and A simultaneously leads to feature entanglement, where shifting emotion breaks the underlying action. To avoid this, three separate Transformer denoisers—an action prior, a valence prior, and an arousal prior—are trained independently over the shared latent space.

During inference, an extended Classifier-Free Guidance composition rule linearly combines the guidance vectors (differences in clean latent predictions) from the three priors. Because the text prior governs "what" is performed while the V and A priors orthogonally modulate "how" it is performed, users can smoothly adjust affective nuance without corrupting the action.

The dataset (III-D) aggregates motions retargeted from AMASS and video with robot teleoperation data. These are categorized into 15 action classes, uniformly sampled, interpolated, and filtered through simulation tracking to retain only physically executable trajectories.

captions.F3: Russell's V-A plane realized on the robot. The horizontal axis represents Valence (postural expansion) and the vertical axis represents Arousal (movement energy and dynamics). Each quadrant visualizes emotions like happy, tense, bored, and sad through full-body poses and motion dynamics.

sections.heading: Does the Intended Emotion Reach Humans? Validation on Hardware and Raters
sections.summary: The authors evaluated V-A tracking fidelity, motion quality, and real-time inference speed, and achieved an emotion recognition rate comparable to human actors in a user study. Ablation studies further confirm the benefits of composable diffusion.
sections.details:
The evaluation used a customized evaluation model for the Unitree G1 to measure motion fidelity and diversity. Compared to text-only baselines (TextOp, ECHO), conditioning on V-A did not degrade motion quality metrics like FID and R-precision, and actually improved MultiModality (diversity within the same class). While the style-reference baseline SMooDi suffered a sharp drop in action retrieval accuracy (R@1 down to 0.166) when style strength was increased, the proposed method maintained around 0.79, preserving the action semantics intact.

In V-A tracking tests, the rank correlation between commanded and remeasured values reached 0.95, confirming monotonic control across the entire range. Cross-axis correlation remained below 0.06, indicating clean orthogonality where changing Valence does not inadvertently drag Arousal. For inference speed, 10 denoising steps took just 78 ms on an RTX 5090, comfortably achieving real-time execution for 400 ms motion primitives.

A perceptual user study (IV-C) crossed 7 actions with 8 emotion categories. Twelve raters watched videos of the robot's motion and guessed the emotion in an 8-way forced choice. The proposed method scored a Top-1 identification rate of 0.384 (chance: 0.125) and a Top-3 rate of 0.845 (chance: 0.375), outperforming the baselines by a large margin. Even when raters erred, their choices clustered on adjacent emotions along the circumplex (an average of 1.48 steps away), showing that the affective direction was communicated accurately. This closely approaches the 0.44 accuracy reported in prior literature for human actors conveying emotion purely through body movements.

Ablation experiments (IV-D) showed that feeding text and V-A into a single unified model degraded action classification accuracy by more than 20%, justifying the composable architecture. Moreover, running diffusion directly in raw feature space rather than latent space hurt tracking accuracy and caused joint jerk to spike by roughly 40%, proving that the smoothing effect of the MVAE is critical for hardware deployment.

captions.F4: The web interface used in the perceptual study. The candidate motion was presented side-by-side with a neutral baseline motion. Participants dragged and dropped their top 3 choices from 8 emotion labels and rated motion naturalness on a 5-point scale.

sections.heading: Expressive Potential and Low-Level Control Challenges
sections.summary: Calibrating the weighting of individual affect metrics and closing the feedback loop between the high-level generator and the low-level whole-body controller are highlighted as key future directions.
sections.details:
Currently, the three metrics for Valence (arm expansion, root height, torso pitch) and the two metrics for Arousal (velocity, acceleration) are summed with equal weights. While this aligns well with psychological findings, optimizing the contribution of each kinematic cue remains an open question for future work.

In addition, the system architecture operates as an open-loop hierarchy: the generative model outputs target trajectories, and a low-level whole-body tracker (the SONIC controller) tracks them. Because the controller has no internal representation of affect, physical tracking errors can cause the remeasured V-A values of the physical robot to drift from the commanded inputs. Closing this loop with feedback on execution state will be important to guarantee that intended affect is reliably preserved under real-world dynamics.

sections.heading: Grounding Emotion in Kinematics for Controllable Humanoids
sections.summary: PAMoR shows that humanoid affective expression can be controlled accurately in real time using V-A coordinates computed directly from body kinematics, eliminating the need for human annotation.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that high-level affective concepts can be modeled through objective, geometrically measurable physical movement parameters. By separating the action prior from the affect priors within a composable diffusion architecture, the robot can freely modulate affective nuance without destabilizing or distorting its core task execution.

Looking ahead, combining this framework with high-level reasoning modules that observe surrounding humans and environments via cameras to dynamically set V-A coordinates will pave the way toward more natural and interactive social humanoids.

takeaways: Qualitative concepts like emotion can be controlled accurately without manual annotation by grounding them in geometric and physical metrics such as postural expansion and movement energy.

Training text (content) and continuous scalars (style) together in a single diffusion model causes negative interference; composable diffusion, which trains independent priors in a shared latent space and fuses them at sampling, avoids this issue effectively.
Even without facial expressions, a humanoid robot can communicate intended emotions to human observers at a level approaching professional human actors simply by modulating body posture and dynamics.
limitations: Because postural expansion, velocity, and acceleration are summed with equal weights, the exact perceptual contribution of each movement feature to emotion recognition is not strictly optimized.

The open-loop setup, where a low-level tracking controller follows generated trajectories without affect awareness, can allow physical affect parameters to drift due to tracking lag or external disturbances.
For actions with strong built-in semantics or aggressive priors (such as punching or kicking), superimposing positive emotional valence remains significantly more challenging.
